item.title: GDOL extends In-School Youth Program application deadline to Oct. 30
item.description: The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi. The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi.

The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.

The program offers eligible 11th-grade students professional development, communications, customer service, and leadership training, along with paid employment opportunities. It has also expanded to include students enrolled in GCC’s Career and Technical Education program.

Participants take part in a two-week winter session and a one-week spring session before completing six weeks of paid summer employment with private-sector employers in fields or industries that interest them. All sessions provide a stipend.

To qualify, students must be in the 11th grade or be part of the GCC Career and Technical Education program and meet other program eligibility requirements.

Interested students can apply online at bit.ly/inschoolyouth or contact their school counselor for more information.

For assistance, contact the American Job Center at 671-475-7500 or email ajc.training@dol.guam.gov . Additional information about the department’s youth program is available at dol.guam.gov .

item.title: Breaking Wave Theatre redirects show proceeds to Typhoon Champi recovery
item.description: Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi. The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.
item.content:encoded:
Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi.

The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.

Originally planned as a fundraiser for the company’s year-round arts programming, the focus shifted after members volunteered with World Central Kitchen and witnessed the needs of families affected by the storm.

The company has also replaced its original $50 admission price with pay-what-you-can tickets ranging from $10 to $50. All ticket levels provide the same experience. Those facing financial barriers to attending can contact events@bwtcguam.com . Individuals and businesses interested in sponsoring tickets for others may also reach out to the organization.

The live tabletop roleplaying show will feature a group of adventurers building a fantasy story through improvisation, character decisions, and dice rolls guided by Game Master James Aevermann.

The event is intended for audiences ages 18 and older. Tickets are available through Guam Time Events.

item.title: CNMI governor seeks revenue sharing, safeguards in seabed mining proposal
item.description: Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands. In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration
item.content:encoded:
Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands.

In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration, Apatang said he recognizes and supports President Donald Trump's goal of reducing U.S. dependence on foreign sources of critical minerals used in technology, clean energy, transportation, health care and defense industries. However, he said national supply-chain objectives should not outweigh potential impacts on CNMI residents and the marine environment.

"The CNMI cannot evaluate the proposed lease sale solely on the basis of national mineral supply chain security objectives and dominance," Apatang wrote, adding that any decision should balance national interests with the well-being of CNMI residents and marine ecosystems.

The governor's comments were submitted in response to the proposed leasing notice for Pacific Minerals Lease Sale 2, or PACM-2, which would make portions of the Outer Continental Shelf around the CNMI available for critical mineral exploration and development.

Apatang noted that more than 65,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier federal information-gathering process and said all should be considered, particularly those expressing concerns about potential environmental harm from deep-sea mining. He said residents have voiced strong opposition to offshore mining and emphasized the longstanding cultural and personal connection indigenous island communities have with the ocean.

The governor also encouraged federal officials to pause the leasing process until two pending federal court cases in Hawaii have been resolved, arguing that proceeding before judicial review is completed could prove inefficient and costly.

In an 11-page letter, Apatang outlined numerous questions and recommendations for federal officials, including whether the CNMI would receive a share of lease revenues and what economic benefits would flow to the Commonwealth if mining activities move forward. He also called for enforceable commitments on local hiring, procurement, workforce development, and infrastructure investments.

The governor further requested additional environmental baseline studies addressing deep-sea coral communities, seamount ecosystems, fisheries, marine mammals, sediment plumes, underwater noise and other potential impacts. He proposed creating a CNMI Marine Minerals Environmental Monitoring Program funded by leaseholders.

Among other recommendations, Apatang sought fisheries compensation mechanisms, protections for cultural and traditional resources, stronger financial assurance requirements, emergency-response funding, safeguards against excessive concentration of lease ownership and restrictions on foreign control of strategically important mineral resources.

He also asked federal officials to clarify how offshore mineral activities would be coordinated with military operations in the Mariana Islands Range Complex and requested a formal framework for continued CNMI participation in future review and permitting processes.

Apatang said the CNMI remains willing to work with federal agencies to identify what he described as a responsible path forward, but stressed that residents should not bear disproportionate environmental, economic or infrastructure-related costs associated with offshore mineral development. He acknowledged that many residents favor a more direct alternative.

"The alternative, as voiced by many CNMI residents, is no mining at all," Apatang wrote

item.title: A D.C. park was made 'for the pleasure of the people.' Trump's plan would change that
item.description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Trump's express wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links has thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — President Trump's express wish to take over the East Potomac Golf Links has thrust a municipal D.C. golf course into the national spotlight. But locals rely on that area for much more than golfing — and worry the district could lose an invaluable recreational oasis.

The southern tip of East Potomac Park, known as Hains Point, is beloved by cyclists, runners, picnickers and birders for its waterfront views, cherry trees and Ohio Drive, the scenic three-mile loop around its perimeter. Runners use the wide, flat road to train; it's even a fixture of several major race courses, including the Marine Corps Marathon on Sunday.

"It's such an important part of the fabric of this region, even though it's not very well known [beyond it]," said Elizabeth Kiker, the executive director of the Washington Area Bicyclists Association. She herself took her now-husband on a bike ride on their second date 20 years ago.

Locals describe Hains Point as a rare public resource in D.C. It's easily accessible from the National Mall yet removed from the crowds, full of people but free of traffic. Congress created it in 1897 , "to be forever held and used as a park for the recreation and pleasure of the people."

And yet, under the president's proposed golf course redesign, Hains Point as people know and love it may cease to exist.

Trump said on Truth Social last weekend that renovations would keep the entire park closed for 15 months starting in November. But it's not clear what would be left when it reopens: The rendering he posted shows an 18-hole course spanning the entire peninsula — including the current playground and picnic area on its southern tip — with no road visible around the perimeter.

The White House referred NPR to the Department of the Interior, which did not respond to NPR's questions about whether those features would be removed as part of the redesign. The proposed renovations have so far been the subject of mixed messages from the administration: Trump said last weekend that work would begin in mid-November, then "immediately." But government lawyers said in court Monday that they were not aware of a final plan .

Even so, the government abruptly downed hundreds of trees on the course with little warning earlier this month, which critics worry was a pretext for beginning renovations. (The government says it was following up on recommendations from a 2019 landscaping report.) Judge Ana Reyes held a hearing on Monday to learn more about the tree-clearing and decide whether to block further work on the golf course.

But it's not just the golf course that's at stake, as a group called Hains Point Runners told Reyes in the courtroom and a written brief. In its 35-page brief, the group says federal law requires the National Park Service to identify and consider the "longstanding recreational uses of the Hains Point corridor" and ways to avoid harming those uses, before embarking on any work that would change it.

"From the perspective of the running community, that did not occur here," lawyers wrote.

Ashley Hawkins of Prince George's County, Md., runs at Hains Point every day, even in the snow. She especially loves the river view and people watching: the families with fishing poles, binocular-wielding birders, people taking a leisurely drive.

"Running is so tied to my mental health," Hawkins said on a recent sunny morning, stretching before she hit the road. "And no place in this area has given me the peace that Hains Point has."

Hawkins has been following the headlines about her beloved running route. While she says she's still in denial about its potential closure, she sees the prospect as part of a pattern of Trump "bypassing" courts to advance his construction projects .

"But to me, this feels the most egregious, because he's taking away public space and trying to make it private," she says. "It feels like one of the more king-like things that he's done so far."

Trump's proposal would combine the park's three historic — and historically affordable — courses into one 18-hole "championship-style" course, which has already raised concerns about who will be able to play on it. Trump has said on Truth Social the golf course will "be open to the Public" while also able to host "world class tournaments" such as the U.S. Open and PGA Championship. He's called the current course "dilapidated, and of no further use or effect," dubbing part of it " Trash Island ."

Each spring, when D.C.'s iconic cherry blossoms bloom, Hains Point is a fan-favorite viewing spot for both locals and tourists. The annual Credit Union Cherry Blossom 10-mile run takes roughly 20,000 participants around the peninsula for that very reason.

But race organizers are looking into backup options for next year given the rumored renovations, event director Rob Wolfe told NPR.

In an email to prospective runners earlier this year, the organization said both the proposed golf course renovations and Trump's planned arch on nearby Arlington Memorial Bridge could significantly alter the course. It urged people to share their concerns with lawmakers and the National Park Service.

Wolfe said the best race experience includes as many cherry blossoms as possible — ideally the ones that frame the park. But, he says, the park's future is "more important than our Sunday in April or Marine Corps Marathon's Sunday in October."

"It's really important that people understand that if this roadway goes away, hundreds, thousands of people on a daily basis would lose out," he said.

Luke Cancilla, a runner and physical therapist who works primarily with endurance runners and cyclists, said Hains Point is a particularly safe environment because there are fewer obstacles such as traffic, stoplights and sidewalks. He often recommends it for people who are starting out or returning after an injury.

"It's open to all of us, which makes it so unique," he said. "You don't have to have an experience level … or be intimated to go out there."

Summer Delehanty, an avid birder, found out about Hains Point when she moved to the area for work about a year ago. She said it's played a huge role in building her D.C. community.

"I've only been here a year, but I still have so many fond memories of going there," she said. "I was there January 1st looking for the snowy owl … I've been there on super hot days, I've picnicked there."

Delehanty has spotted all kinds of birds at that park, including rarities such as the fork-tailed flycatcher. She said Hains Point is a uniquely great birdwatching spot in the district because of its position right along the Potomac River: People have a 360-degree view of the migrating birds that fly overhead or take shelter in the trees.

"There's nothing else in D.C. like it," she said, adding that she's not sure where regular birders would go instead. They could perhaps get similar views from the Virginia side of the river, she said, but those wouldn't count as D.C. bird sightings.

The Trump administration cut down 430 of the park's trees earlier this month, with less than a day's notice. That means fewer places for tired birds to rest, Delehanty says, and potentially fewer birds stopping by altogether. And, if the park is closed to humans, there won't be anyone there to track the species that do, which she said is important for conservation purposes.

María-Elena Montero, president of the D.C. Bird Alliance, says the potential closure of Hains Point would mean a "devastating loss of habitat" for birds and humans alike.

"It belongs to the people," she said. "And to lose that aspect of being able to experience such a gorgeous space right in the middle of the city, right in the shadow of an airport and monuments … is a big loss for everybody."

Last October, the Trump administration started dumping debris from another controversial construction project — the demolition of the White House East Wing — on the grounds of the golf course. In February, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers sued the government in an effort to stop what they describe as an unlawful takeover of a public course.

item.title: 'Possible Love' offers four of the best performances you'll see all year
item.description: The writer-director Lee Chang-dong belongs to a rare breed of filmmakers who have never made anything less than a great movie. Not surprisingly, there's sometimes a long wait between those movies: It's been eight years since his previous work, the chilly psychological thriller Burning . It's wonderful to have him back with a new film, Possible Love , which tells a story that's been weighing on him
item.content:encoded:
The writer-director Lee Chang-dong belongs to a rare breed of filmmakers who have never made anything less than a great movie. Not surprisingly, there's sometimes a long wait between those movies: It's been eight years since his previous work, the chilly psychological thriller Burning .

It's wonderful to have him back with a new film, Possible Love , which tells a story that's been weighing on him for some time. It was inspired by an incident from 2009, when a car factory in Korea laid off one-third of its workforce. The metal workers' union organized a strike, which was brutally shut down by police. Many of the workers subsequently took their own lives.

The film, which director Lee co-wrote with Oh Jung-mi, follows a married couple two years after a similar tragedy shook their small industrial town. Sul Kyung-gu plays a welder named Ho-seok, one of many who were laid off from a factory due to a major restructuring.

Ho-seok now has another metalworking job elsewhere, but the pain of his termination still lingers, and he's become an alcoholic. His wife, Mi-ok, played by Jeon Do-yeon, works at a company that manufactures face masks. She's the warm-spirited glue holding the family together; they also have a young son.

Early on, the couple meets a woman named Ye-ji, an aspiring filmmaker who's shooting a documentary about the layoffs. Ye-ji wants them both to appear in the film, but only Mi-ok is game to be interviewed. She reveals a lot about her past on camera: We see flashbacks of her with her mom, who felt ashamed and even angry about their working-class roots. We also see the thrilling day that she and Ho-seok first met, as teenagers.

Ye-ji shares a bit about herself, too, including how she met her very handsome, very rich hedge-fund-investor-type husband. But even as the two women forge a friendship, the flow of information here is largely a one-way street. The film never lets us forget that their bond is governed by clear differences of class, wealth and power. Ye-ji's kindness, genuine as it seems, is conditioned on Mi-ok's ongoing participation in her project.

At times, Possible Love can play like a treatise on documentary ethics. But while Ye-ji's methods certainly warrant critique, director Lee sharply implicates himself as well. His gently handheld camerawork sometimes blurs into Ye-ji's footage, making it hard to tell whose perspective we're seeing. Lee seems to be acknowledging that fictional and nonfictional storytelling both have their manipulations, and he's determined to do right by the real events and real issues that he draws on. Possible Love itself is opening the same month that its distributor, Netflix, laid off a staggering 6% of its global workforce.

There's a documentary-like quality to some of the film's most moving moments, which take place at a group-counseling session for laid-off workers and their spouses. We hear them speak about the joyous early days of the strike, the sense of solidarity that they experienced before it was shut down. Lee's earlier films, like Oasis and Peppermint Candy , have often portrayed misfits and outcasts. In Possible Love , he explores a different kind of alienation, the kind that results from the rupture of a once-great community.

Since its premiere at festivals earlier this fall, Possible Love has sparked a lot of comparisons to Parasite , another class-conscious Korean drama about two families. Cho Yeo-jeong, who played the rich wife in Parasite , is equally terrific as Ye-ji, the rich wife in this film. Yet the two movies are more different than they are similar. Where Parasite was a virtuoso Hitchcockian thriller, Possible Love has an almost novelistic richness and depth of character. It also has four of the year's best performances.

As Ye-ji's husband, Zo In-sung is such a smooth mix of condescension and charm that you might not recognize him from the recent down-and-dirty monster movie Hope . And then there are the leads, Sul and Jeon, both of whom have done some of their best work in Lee's previous films, and who do some of their best work again here. As the depressed and drunken Ho-seok, Sul gives a quietly implosive, deeply mysterious performance; he keeps revealing layers of himself through the final moments.

As for his wife, Mi-ok, she's simply one of the most memorably complex characters you'll see in a movie this year. Remarkably, she hasn't given in to despair. She meets every challenge with a playful sense of mischief, and though she often gets exasperated with her husband, even the way she chides him makes clear the depths of their connection. The title of Possible Love asks whether love can survive life's difficulties. For all their deeply human foibles, Ho-seok and Mi-ok answer that question with a resounding yes.

item.title: 'Clayface' is underbaked body horror
item.description: Clayface is a C-list Batman villain, but Batman doesn't show up at all in the new film Clayface . item.content:encoded:
Clayface is a C-list Batman villain, but Batman doesn't show up at all in the new film Clayface . Turns out there's plenty of precedent for quarantining a supervillain away from their superheroic counterpart and trying to build a movie around them. That ignoble roster includes the Joker and Venom films, alongside Morbius , Kraven the Hunter and Catwoman .

Neither is Clayface even close to the first R-rated movie set in a superheroic universe — that list is even longer: The Jokers again, the Deadpool films, the Blade films, Logan , The Suicide Squad , Dredd , The Crow and The Punisher , plus sundry "mature" meta-commentaries on the superhero archetype like the Kick-Ass films, Watchmen and Super . (It's not even the first superhero-horror mashup — some of us out here in these streets still remember The New Mutants , Brightburn and Chronicle , for our sins.)

What Clayface is, just absurdly specifically, is the first villain-centered, R-rated, body-horror movie.

What it represents to the folks running DC Studios right now is something more abstract: It is a test case. It poses the question: Is the DC Universe large enough to stretch beyond the worrisomely attenuated superhero genre in favor of something more lucrative like horror, a genre whose vise-like grip on the box office shows no sign of weakening?

The answer Clayface provides is: No. Not yet, at least.

That's because the film gets stuck, planting one of its feet of clay in horror and the other in superhero, and completely fails to move. Sure, there's plenty of gross-out body horror stuff involving blades slicing through skin, flesh, organs and eyelids. If your idea of a great night at the movies is watching too, too solid flesh melt, thaw and resolve itself into a goo, you're in luck.

But there's not enough of it to satisfy diehard fans of such seriously squelchy fare, because at its semi-solid heart, Clayface assiduously adheres to the superhero movie formula: Adversity happens. Powers manifest. Justice is served.

(It's perhaps more correct to call it a super- anti hero movie formula, as it's not technically justice that gets served, but revenge.) (Revenge, as far as Hollywood is concerned, is justice with arterial spray.)

The plot is thin but effective: Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) is a hot young movie star on top of the world, until a run-in with a painfully generic mob boss (David Dencik) leaves him disfigured. Desperate for a solution, he seeks out a scientist (Naomi Ackie) who's developing an untested procedure involving nanotechnology that can merge with Matt's body. Said nanotech is powered by AI, so nothing could possibly go wrong.

Kidding: Plenty of face-melty, body-morphy, splurty-squicky-slimy hijinks dutifully ensue, and Matt metes out his loamy vengeance on all who wronged him.

Clayface 's horror elements work well in the early going, when Matt starts having trouble keeping his symmetrical, Tom-of-Finland facial features from going all late-period Picasso on him. But as his superpowers manifest, the film abandons the horror of the uncanny valley for the whiz-bang of the comic book splash page. To this fan of superhero stuff, that's not a complaint, but I could sense my fellow, more bloodthirsty theater-goers growing increasingly restless.

To its credit, Clayface is not a long movie, and starts putting its pieces in place and setting them in motion immediately. The amount of time it takes for Matt's world to crumble around him, for instance, is so hilariously truncated it feels like the filmmakers were worried about our attention span.

But that pacing does make sense: Clayface isn't a character study, or a meditation on the superficiality of beauty standards and fame (though the screenplay flirts with both ideas). No, it's a revenge movie.

Scratch that, it's a revenge flick . And the flicks to which it's most deeply indebted — think Oldboy , and Kill Bill Vols. 1 and 2 , and the John Wick franchise — they're not about weaving layers of characterization and parsing psychological nuance. No, they're about creating tension and releasing it as rapidly as possible. Delivering chunk after satisfying chunk of (literally) visceral thrills and catharsis.

But those other films — and Sam Raimi's 1990 film Darkman , to which this movie owes a narrative debt so huge it could wipe out several Baltic nations — all possess something Clayface lacks, which is style for days. Visual flair. Aesthetic idiosyncrasy. (And in the case of Darkman : A charming, heedless goofiness.) The Gotham of Clayface is not the mysterious, goth-inflected urban hellscape of any Batman movie you care to name, it's just … Liverpool. (DC Studios co-lead James Gunn has made it clear that director Matt Reeves' The Batman films exist separately from this DCU.)

If Clayface doesn't quite work as a proof-of-concept for DC horror as a viable ongoing concern, it's effective as an opening gambit in what will assuredly prove a long game. Like its protagonist, the film shoots out its goopy, mud-brown, protoplasmic feelers into the undiscovered territory of horror, but it does so too tentatively, and is too quick to retract them the moment it meets resistance.

And that's a shame. Clayface could have done something surprising, something new, if only it'd had the courage to go in for the kiln.

This piece also appeared in NPR's Pop Culture Happy Hour newsletter. Sign up for the newsletter so you don't miss the next one, plus get weekly recommendations about what's making us happy.

Listen to Pop Culture Happy Hour on Apple Podcasts and Spotify .

item.title: Ex-FBI employees charged with lying to Congress over Hunter Biden inquiries
item.description: Updated October 24, 2026 at 4:50 AM ChST The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees with making false statements to Congress in connection with the bureau's investigations into Hunter Biden and his laptop ahead of the 2020 presidential election.
item.content:encoded:
Updated October 24, 2026 at 4:50 AM ChST

The Justice Department has charged two former FBI employees with making false statements to Congress in connection with the bureau's investigations into Hunter Biden and his laptop ahead of the 2020 presidential election.

Bradley Benavides and Nikki Floris each face a single criminal count stemming from testimony before lawmakers in 2023. The pair, who held senior positions on the FBI's now defunct Foreign Influence Task Force, both turned themselves in and made their initial court appearance Friday morning in Washington, D.C.

The new prosecution is the latest politically fraught case to be brought by the Justice Department since President Trump returned to the White House. It dredges back up the bizarre saga surrounding former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, and his various legal troubles that featured throughout the 2020 presidential campaign.

Hunter Biden's laptop was the subject of intense scrutiny after The New York Post reported weeks before the 2020 presidential election that the device was abandoned at a Delaware repair shop in 2019, and then obtained by President Trump's former personal lawyer Rudy Giuliani.

Republicans have long accused the FBI of mishandling the laptop and the investigations into the younger Biden. Hunter Biden was convicted of federal gun charges and later pleaded guilty to separate tax offenses. (Joe Biden signed a full and unconditional pardon for his son in December 2024.)

In a statement on X , the U.S. attorney for Washington, D.C., Jeanine Pirro, said Floris and Benavides "allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election."

Prosecutors charged Benavides and Floris by criminal complaint, which means prosecutors have yet to secure an indictment from a grand jury. Under the second Trump administration, grand juries in the nation's capital and other cities have refused on several occasions to return indictments in high-profile, politically charged cases.

At a court hearing Friday morning, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui noted that both of the defendants have "sparkling backgrounds" in federal law enforcement and were longtime dedicated public servants. He also noted that charging them by criminal complaint for conduct that is "quite old" is unusual.

Benavides, 56, and Floris, 46, are due back in court for a preliminary hearing on Tuesday.

In a statement, Floris' attorneys called her a "patriot" who served as "dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years."

"Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they added.

The Post reported Hunter Biden's laptop showed wrongdoing by then-Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who subsequently won the election. Some of the data on the laptop was later ascertained to belong to Hunter Biden. House Republicans subsequently launched an impeachment inquiry into President Biden, focusing on Hunter Biden's business dealings at the time his father was vice president. But no evidence has ever been presented that Joe Biden financially gained from his son's business activities.

The complaint alleges that Benavides and Floris both had real-time knowledge of the Hunter Biden investigations, including into his laptop, in their top posts on the Foreign Influence Task Force.

But in interviews with the House Judiciary Committee in 2023, both of them allegedly lied about their knowledge and involvement in those investigations.

Those purported false statements were material to the committee's investigation, the complaint says, because they allowed both Benavides and Floris to "escape" further questioning about Hunter Biden, which hindered the panel's investigation.
